The crested bigscale Poromitra crassiceps is a mesopelagic fish species for which a comprehensive suite of life-history measurements has been assembled from specimens collected during deepwater trawling surveys in the North Atlantic. Individuals attain a maximum standard length of 14.8 centimeters [Li = 14.8 centimeters], a value that places this species among the larger members of the family Melamphaidae. The relationship between length and body mass in females follows a power-law scaling approximating 0.01000 times length raised to the 3.04 power, yielding an asymptotic wet body mass of 36.1 grams [Wwi = 36.1 grams] for fully grown females. At the other end of the size spectrum, newly hatched larvae emerge from eggs measuring approximately 0.7 millimeters in diameter, which corresponds to a wet weight at birth of just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minute starting mass reflects the relatively small yolk reserves typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts and imposes a substantial energetic challenge on the larva during the transition to exogenous feeding.

Puberty in the crested bigscale is defined by a combination of standard length and body mass thresholds rather than by a strict chronological age, reflecting the strong influence of resource availability on maturation schedules in deep-sea environments. Females typically attain sexual maturity at a standard length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], at which point their wet weight averages approximately 11 grams [Wwp = approximately 11 grams]. This size at maturation is consistent with predictions from the length-mass relationship observed across the species, and it implies that females require roughly two-thirds of their ultimate length before allocating energy toward gamete production. The protracted growth phase leading up to puberty may be an adaptive response to the low and unpredictable food supply characteristic of mesopelagic habitats, where the risk of starvation during reproductive events is substantial and delayed maturation allows for greater somatic capital accumulation.

Reproductive output in Poromitra crassiceps has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate the cold, stable thermal regime of its natural depth range. At a constant temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], females achieve a maximum annual reproductive output that corresponds to approximately 10 eggs per day when extrapolated from short-term observations of spawning frequency and clutch size. This daily rate, while modest in absolute terms, is derived from a combination of frequent spawning events and moderate fecundity per event. The species produces multiple clutches each year, with individual clutches containing a relatively small number of large, yolky eggs that undergo external fertilization following broadcast spawning.

Longevity data for the crested bigscale point to a remarkably extended lifespan relative to its small body size, a pattern that aligns with the general life-history syndrome of slow growth and late maturity observed in many deep-sea fishes. Under the same cold thermal regime of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 8.5 years [am = 8.5 years], which corresponds to approximately 3100 days from hatching to natural death. This extreme longevity is presumably linked to the metabolic constraints imposed by the low ambient temperatures of the mesopelagic zone, where reduced enzymatic reaction rates slow the pace of both somatic growth and physiological senescence. Comparative data from confamilial species suggest that such long lifespans are typical within the Melamphaidae, although the crested bigscale appears to occupy the upper end of the family's longevity distribution.

The early life stages of the crested bigscale are characterized by a lecithotrophic period during which the yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous yolk reserves absorbed within the first days after eclosion. Hatching occurs from pelagic eggs that drift in the upper water column, and the prolarvae emerge at an extremely small size, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. The transition to exogenous feeding is a critical bottleneck: larvae must locate and capture suitable zooplankton prey before their yolk reserves are exhausted, a challenge compounded by the low prey densities typical of the mesopelagic zone. Survivorship during this period is likely very low, consistent with a life-history strategy that relies on high fecundity to compensate for high early mortality.
